papers.title: Quantum walks and conformal mappings
papers.label: arXiv:2611.30403v1

summary.one_liner: The paper derives uniform asymptotic formulas for the wave function of the discrete quantum walk (Feynman checkers, six-vertex model with special complex weights) across the whole space-time plane, using conformal mappings to handle Airy- and gamma-function transitions.
summary.plain: The paper studies a simple discrete model of a quantum particle, an electron hopping step by step along a line, and asks how its wave function behaves at every position and time. It finds the expected change between wavy and fading behaviour, described by the Airy function, and a second change near the speed of light, described by the gamma function. The authors prove two general theorems giving single formulas valid across these transitions, using a change of coordinates in the complex plane.
summary.why: Exact, uniform formulas that work across transition regions are useful tools for quantum walks, which appear in quantum computing and physics models, and the authors say the methods apply to other situations. The text does not establish wider impact beyond this, so its reach outside this setting is uncertain.
summary.background:
- Quantum walk: the discrete, step-by-step analogue of a quantum particle moving randomly, with amplitudes rather than probabilities.
- Wave function: a complex-valued function whose squared size gives the probability of finding the particle at a position.
- Asymptotic formula: an approximation that becomes accurate for large distances or times.
- Airy function: a special function describing the boundary between oscillating and exponentially decaying behaviour.
- Gamma function: a standard special function generalising factorials, here governing behaviour near the maximal speed.
- Conformal mapping: a smooth change of variables in the complex plane that preserves angles, used to simplify integrals.
- Six-vertex model: a lattice model from statistical physics, here with special complex weights.

papers.abstract: We study the most elementary discrete model of an electron moving along a line, known as Feynman checkers, quantum walk, or the six-vertex model with special complex weights, and provide a uniform asymptotic formula for the wave function in the whole xt-plane. In addition to the well-known appearance of the Airy function that describes the transition between the oscillating and exponentially decaying regimes, we observe a second transition governed by the gamma function when the electron speed approaches the speed of light. We prove two general theorems producing uniform asymptotic formulae involving the Airy and gamma functions, using conformal mappings associated with the underlying integral representations. They are applicable in several other situations as well.

papers.title: Central limit theorem for energies of determinantal point processes on complex manifolds I
papers.label: arXiv:2611.31229v1

summary.one_liner: The paper proves a central limit theorem for the Green energy, and for the logarithmic energy, of Bergman determinantal point processes on compact Riemann surfaces and complex manifolds, using local Bergman kernel asymptotics and a cumulant expansion.
summary.plain: The paper studies random arrangements of N points on a curved complex surface, where the points are shaped by a probabilistic rule that discourages them from clustering. For a measure of how the points interact, called the Green energy, it gives the typical size of that quantity and its spread. It then shows that, once N is large, the fluctuations of this energy behave like the familiar bell-shaped (Gaussian) curve.
summary.why: Central limit theorems tell us when random fluctuations become predictable, which matters for understanding how well such random point models can be tested or simulated. The text does not say what wider applications it has, so its broader significance is uncertain from this excerpt alone.
summary.background:
- Point process: a random collection of points, here N points on a surface.
- Determinantal point process: a random point model where correlations are governed by a kernel (a function describing how strongly points relate), which tends to spread points apart.
- Bergman kernel and positive line bundle: geometric objects on complex surfaces that define the point model.
- Riemann surface: a one-dimensional complex surface, such as a sphere or torus.
- Green function and energy: the Green function measures influence between two points; the energy sums this over all pairs of points.
- U-statistic: an average over all pairs of sample points.
- Cumulants: summary quantities of a random variable; a central limit theorem is shown by controlling them.
- Central limit theorem: the statement that suitably normalized sums of random quantities approach a bell curve.

papers.abstract: We study the Bergman determinantal point process associated with a positive line bundle on a compact Riemann surface. Consider the U-statistic given by the Green function, called the Green energy. For a configuration of $N$ points, the expectation of Green energy is $\frac12 N\log N+O(N)$, and the variance is $(\log 2-\pi^2/24)N+O(\log^2 N)$. We prove a central limit theorem for the Green energy by combining local Bergman kernel asymptotics with an expansion for the cumulants. A central limit theorem also holds for the logarithmic energy of Bergman determinantal point process on complex manifolds.

papers.title: An affine surface with 3-step nilpotent fundamental group
papers.label: arXiv:2611.27475v1

summary.background:
- Complex affine surface: a smooth solution set of polynomial equations in two complex variables, with the points at infinity removed.
- Fundamental group: a group recording which loops on a space can be continuously deformed into one another.
- Nilpotent group: a group that becomes trivial after repeatedly taking commutators; "k-step nilpotent" measures how many such levels are needed.
- Virtually nilpotent: the group has a finite-index subgroup that is nilpotent.
- Campana's nilpotency problem: a conjectural link between the loop structure of a space and its nilpotency, asked in the projective and quasi-projective settings.
- Quasi-projective: a space that is an open subset of a projective (compact-type) algebraic variety.
summary.one_liner: The paper constructs a smooth complex affine surface whose fundamental group is virtually 3-step nilpotent but not virtually 2-step nilpotent, giving a negative answer to the quasi-projective version of Campana's nilpotency problem.
summary.plain: The paper is about the shapes that complex algebraic surfaces can have, as seen through their "loops" (the fundamental group, a way of recording which closed paths can be deformed into one another). The author builds a specific smooth surface of this kind whose loop structure is nested three levels deep but not two, which settles a question in the negative.
summary.why: The result answers a specific open question (a version of Campana's nilpotency problem) by showing the answer is no in the quasi-projective setting. Beyond that, the text does not say more about wider implications, so its significance beyond this question is unclear from the summary alone.

papers.abstract: We construct a smooth complex affine surface $Y$ such that $\pi_1(Y)$ is virtually $3$-step nilpotent, but not virtually $2$-step nilpotent. This gives a negative answer to the quasi-projective version of Campana's nilpotency problem.

papers.title: Local connectivity of Julia sets of Newton maps of trigonometric and hyperbolic functions
papers.label: arXiv:2611.26654v1

summary.background:
- Newton's method: an iterative rule for approximating roots of an equation; each starting point is mapped step by step.
- Julia set: the boundary between starting points whose iterates behave tamely and those that behave chaotically.
- Basin of attraction: the set of starting points that converge to a given attracting point; "immediate" means the component touching that point directly.
- Transcendental meromorphic function: a complex function that is not a polynomial or rational function, with poles allowed, such as sin or cos.
- Local connectivity: a topological property saying the boundary is not pinched in a way that makes it hard to approach locally; here it is stated for the boundary of each basin.
- Repelling petal: a region near infinity where iteration pushes points away, used as a technical tool.
- Affine conjugacy: two maps are the same up to a linear change of coordinates.
summary.one_liner: The paper proves local connectivity of Julia sets (the boundaries between stable and chaotic behaviour) for Newton maps of sin, cos, sinh and cosh, by verifying repelling petals at infinity for the cosine map and showing the hyperbolic family is affinely conjugate to the sine case.
summary.plain: The paper studies a method for finding roots of equations, called Newton's method, applied to four standard trigonometric and hyperbolic functions, and asks how the boundary between starting points that converge and those that do not is shaped. The authors show that for the cosine version, certain half-plane regions far from the origin behave in a way that lets an existing mathematical criterion apply, giving a clean boundary shape. They also show that a whole family of hyperbolic functions is, after a change of coordinates, the same as the sine version, so a previously published result covers them too.
summary.why: It settles a structural question about the boundaries of these dynamical systems for a whole family of maps by reducing them to one known case. Its wider relevance is mainly to specialists in complex dynamics; the text does not claim applications beyond that field.

papers.abstract: We study the Newton maps of $\sin z$, $\cos z$, $\sinh z$, and $\cosh z$, each of which is transcendental meromorphic and has infinitely many unbounded immediate attracting basins. We first verify directly that, for the cosine Newton map $N_{\cos}(z) = z + \cot z$, the half-planes $\{\pm \operatorname{Im} z > M\}$ are repelling petals at infinity for every $M \ge 2$. These explicit petals allow us to apply the tame-basin criterion of Bara\'nski, Fagella, Jarque, and Karpi\'nska and obtain local connectivity of the spherical boundary of each immediate basin of $N_{\cos}$. We also show that the Newton map of $Ae^{\lambda z} + Be^{-\lambda z}$, where $AB\lambda \neq 0$, is affinely conjugate to the sine Newton map $N_{\sin}(z) = z - \tan z$. The published local-connectivity theorem for $J(N_{\sin})$ therefore applies to this entire family, including the cosine and the two hyperbolic Newton maps. We describe the invariant lines and basin geometry of the four maps and illustrate the corresponding dynamical planes numerically.

papers.title: On the solution of a question for meromorphic functions sharing three values IM and a fourth value CM in the complex plane
papers.label: arXiv:2611.25948v1

summary.background:
- Meromorphic function: a function of a complex variable that is analytic except for isolated poles (points where it blows up).
- Sharing a value: f and g both take a given value a at the same points.
- CM (counting multiplicity) versus IM (ignoring multiplicity): CM also requires the same order of contact at those points.
- Infinity as a value: the point where a function has a pole, treated as a value in the extended complex plane.
- Nevanlinna theory: the study of how often meromorphic functions take given values, from 1926 onward.
- Gundersen's question (1992): whether sharing three values IM and a fourth CM forces sharing all four CM.
- Only the abstract-level statement is given here; the proof details are not in the text provided.
summary.one_liner: The paper settles Gundersen's long-standing question (1992) on meromorphic functions sharing three values IM and a fourth CM, by proving that when f and g share three finite values IM and infinity CM, they also share the three finite values CM.
summary.plain: The paper concerns pairs of functions defined on the complex numbers that take the same values at the same points. Two functions "share" a value if they hit it at the same places, either with multiplicity counted (CM) or ignoring multiplicity (IM). The author proves that a known open question, whether sharing three values loosely and a fourth value tightly forces tight sharing of all four, has a positive answer in the case described.
summary.why: This question had been open since 1992 and sits at the core of Nevanlinna's value distribution theory, a classical area of mathematics. The text itself does not discuss applications beyond this theory, so its wider significance is uncertain to me.

papers.abstract: In 1926, Nevanlinna (Acta Math. {\bf 48} (1926), no. 3-4, 367-391) proved that if two distinct and non-constant meromorphic functions $f$ and $g$ share $a_1,$ $a_2,$ $a_3,$ $a_4$ CM in the complex plane, where $a_1,$ $a_2,$ $a_3,$ $a_4$ are four distinct complex values in the extended complex plane, then $f$ is a Möbius transformation of $g$, two of the shared values, say $a_1$ and $a_2$, are Picard exceptional values, and the cross ratio $\left(a_1, a_2, a_3, a_4\right)=-1.$ Later on, Gundersen (Trans. Amer. Math. Soc. {\bf 277} (1983), no. 2, 545-567. Correction: {\bf 304} (1987), 847-850) proved that if two non-constant meromorphic functions share two values CM and share two other values IM, then the functions share all four values CM. In 1992, Gundersen (Complex Var. Elliptic Equ. {\bf 20} (1992), no. 1-4, 99-106) proposed the following famous question: if two non-constant meromorphic functions share three distinct values IM and share a fourth value CM, then do the functions necessarily share all four values CM? This question is a long-standing question in the studies of the Nevanlinna's value distribution theory of meromorphic functions, and has not been completely resolved by now. In this paper, we completely resolve the question, and prove that if two distinct and non-constant meromorphic functions $f$ and $g$ share $a_1,$ $a_2,$ $a_3$ IM and $\infty$ CM, where $a_1,$ $a_2,$ $a_3$ are three distinct and finite complex values in the complex plane, then $f$ and $g$ also share $a_1,$ $a_2,$ $a_3$ CM.

papers.title: Matrix-point interpolation for positive real odd functions in one and several variables
papers.label: arXiv:2611.26240v1

summary.background:
- Complex analysis: functions of a complex variable, defined on the complex plane.
- Right half-plane: the set of complex numbers with positive real part.
- Positive real function: a function whose values have nonnegative real part on the half-plane; these model passive physical or electrical systems.
- Interpolation: finding a function that takes prescribed values at prescribed points.
- Matrix-valued function: outputs are grids of numbers rather than single numbers.
- Pole at infinity: a point where the function's size grows without bound as the input goes to infinity.
- Noncommutative multivariable setting: several inputs whose order of multiplication matters, as with matrices.
summary.one_liner: The paper studies matrix-point interpolation for positive real matrix-valued functions on the right half-plane, in both single-variable and noncommutative multivariable settings, with attention to when a pole at infinity can or must occur.
summary.plain: The paper looks at a problem of finding a smooth function with prescribed values at given points, where the function's outputs are grids of numbers (matrices) and the function must stay "positive" on a half of the complex plane. The authors analyse when the solution may or must blow up at infinity in the one-variable case. In the multivariable case, where the structure at infinity is more complicated, they restrict to solutions that do not blow up there.
summary.why: Problems of this kind arise in systems and control theory and in operator theory, where positive real functions describe passive systems. The text says the results also yield numerical algorithms for computing a solution, but it does not give details of those algorithms or their performance, so the practical reach is unclear from this text alone.

papers.abstract: We study the single matrix point interpolation problem for positive real matrix valued functions on the right half-plane, both in the single variable setting and in the noncommutative multivariable setting. In the single variable case, a careful analysis is done for when the solution may or must have a pole at infinity. In the multivariable setting, as the pole structure at infinity can be more complicated, we focus on the case when there is no pole at infinity. The results also yield numerical algorithms for finding a solution.

papers.title: The Holomorphic Reduction of Pseudoconvex Homogeneous Manifolds
papers.label: arXiv:2611.24922v1

summary.background:
- Complex manifold: a space that locally looks like complex-number coordinates, with holomorphic (complex-differentiable) functions on it.
- Complex Lie group and homogeneous space G/H: a group of complex symmetries G acting transitively on the space, with H the stabiliser of a point.
- Pseudoconvex: a shape condition, here defined by the existence of a continuous plurisubharmonic exhaustion function (a function that grows to infinity toward the edge and is "convex" in complex directions).
- Holomorphic reduction: the largest quotient of the space that still separates its holomorphic functions, so that it has the same holomorphic functions as the original.
- Stein space: a complex space that is holomorphically separable and has good cohomological properties; it is the complex analogue of an affine variety.
- Holomorphically separable: any two distinct points can be told apart by some holomorphic function.
summary.one_liner: For a pseudoconvex homogeneous complex manifold G/H (G a connected complex Lie group, H a closed complex subgroup), the paper shows that the holomorphic reduction G/J is Stein and that the fibre J/H carries no non-constant holomorphic functions.
summary.plain: The paper studies a certain kind of smooth space built from a symmetry group acting on a complex space, where the space is "pseudoconvex," a shape condition on how its boundary-like behaviour can be measured. It starts from a known result that such a space can be simplified by a canonical quotient, called the holomorphic reduction, which keeps all its complex-valued functions. The authors show that, under the pseudoconvexity assumption, this simplified quotient is a Stein space (a especially well-behaved type of complex space) and that the leftover piece has only constant complex functions.
summary.why: The result sharpens the general picture of how homogeneous complex spaces decompose, which is a structural question in complex geometry. The text itself does not describe applications beyond this classification-style statement, so its wider significance is unclear from the excerpt.

papers.abstract: Suppose $G$ is a connected complex Lie group and $H$ is a closed complex subgroup. Then there exists a closed complex subgroup $J$ of $G$ containing $H$ such that the fibration $π:G/H \to G/J$ is the holomorphic reduction of $G/H$, i.e., $G/J$ is holomorphically separable and ${\mathcal O}(G/H) \cong π^*{\mathcal O}(G/J)$. In this paper we prove that if $G/H$ is pseudoconvex, i.e., if $G/H$ admits a continuous plurisubharmonic exhaustion function, then $G/J$ is Stein and $J/H$ has no non-constant holomorphic functions.

papers.title: Recent developments in stochastic systems with singular dynamics -- a brief survey --
papers.label: arXiv:2611.24610v1

summary.background:
- Stochastic differential equation: an equation describing motion with random noise, such as a particle jiggling while being pushed by a force (the "drift").
- Singular drift: a force that becomes infinitely strong or undefined at certain points, so the usual smoothness assumptions fail.
- Interacting particle system: many randomly moving objects whose motion depends on each other.
- Symmetric polynomials: polynomials unchanged when variables are swapped; used here as a tool to handle the equations.
- Loewner chain / Schramm-Loewner evolution: a family of growing random curves in the plane, used in modeling random shapes such as boundaries of random clusters.
- Random matrices: matrices with random entries, whose eigenvalues often form interacting particle systems.
summary.one_liner: An expository survey of stochastic differential equations with singular drifts, covering symmetric-polynomial methods and their links to multiple Schramm-Loewner evolutions, random matrices, and machine learning.
summary.plain: This is an overview paper about random motion of interacting particles whose governing equations blow up or behave badly at certain points, so standard mathematical tools do not directly apply. The author surveys several models and the methods used to study them, especially an approach based on symmetric polynomials. The text also points to connections with random curves, random matrices, and machine learning, though it is a survey rather than a report of new results.
summary.why: Particle systems with singular interactions show up in several areas of probability and mathematical physics, so a consolidated map of methods and links may help newcomers. The text does not state specific new theorems, so its value is mainly as an orientation guide, and I cannot judge from the abstract how complete the coverage is.

papers.abstract: Diffusions with singular drifts appear naturally in the study of certain classes of interesting particle systems. Due to the singularities involved in the equations describing them, studying their dynamics is both interesting and challenging as they fall outside of the usual regularity assumptions on the vector fields in the literature. One needs to introduce and study them with different methods, with the use of symmetric polynomials being a particularly promising approach. In this expository work, we give an overview of some models and methods, and we further explore their interactions with the areas of Multiple Loewner chains (in particular, multiple Schramm-Loewner Evolutions), the new links with Random Matrices, and the novel area of Machine Learning for Singular Dynamics.

papers.title: A Quasiconformal Squeezing function and Fridman invariant and applications
papers.label: arXiv:2611.22677v1

summary.background:
- Domain: an open connected region in space (here, in the complex plane or in R^n).
- Conformal map: a smooth map that preserves angles locally; quasiconformal maps are allowed to distort angles by a bounded amount K.
- Biholomorphic invariant: a quantity unchanged by one-to-one holomorphic (complex-differentiable) maps between domains, used to classify domains.
- Squeezing function: measures how well a domain can be mapped into the unit ball, giving a number between 0 and 1.
- Fridman invariant: a related biholomorphic invariant built from the domain's geometry.
- Spherically extreme point: a boundary point where the domain locally looks like a ball in a extremal sense; used to study boundary behaviour.
- Ferrand–Obata and Wong–Rosay theorems: rigidity results saying that certain conformal or holomorphic maps are forced to be special (ball-like) when a boundary or invariant condition holds.
summary.one_liner: The paper defines quasiconformal (angle-distorting, conformal-type) analogues of the squeezing function and Fridman invariant, studies their basic properties and boundary behaviour, relates them to each other, and proves variants of the Ferrand–Obata theorem for domains in R^n.
summary.plain: This paper is about shape measurements of regions in space, of the kind used in complex analysis. The authors build new versions of two existing measurements that work when you allow a controlled amount of distortion in the mapping rather than requiring perfect conformal (angle-preserving) maps. They then check how these new measures behave, show they are related to each other, and use them to state and prove versions of a known rigidity theorem for regions in ordinary n-dimensional space.
summary.why: The squeezing function and Fridman invariant are established tools for telling domains apart and for studying their boundaries, so extending them to quasiconformal maps widens that toolkit to settings beyond complex structure. The stated link between the Ferrand–Obata and Wong–Rosay theorems suggests a useful parallel, though the text alone does not show how far the results reach beyond the authors' own statements.

papers.abstract: The squeezing function and Fridman invariant are two examples of biholomorphic invariants that have proved to be useful in exploring questions in complex geometry. Motivated by their construction, we define conformal analogues of these invariants by using suitable families of $K$-quasiconformal mappings, and study several basic properties such as continuity, domain dependence and boundary behaviour near spherically extreme points. It is also shown that these conformal invariants are explicitly related. As an application, we propose and prove variants of the Ferrand--Obata theorem in conformal geometry that apply to domains in $\mbb R^n$. This highlights the close analogy that exists between the Ferrand--Obata and Wong--Rosay theorems.

papers.title: A Burns-Krantz theorem on convex domains
papers.label: arXiv:2611.22516v1

summary.background:
- Holomorphic map: a smooth map between complex spaces that respects complex structure; roughly, a complex-differentiable function applied to several complex variables.
- Bounded convex domain: a bounded region of complex n-dimensional space with no dents in its boundary.
- Self-map: a map sending the region into itself.
- Identity map: the map that leaves every point fixed.
- Boundary rigidity: the idea that behaviour at a single boundary point severely restricts the whole map.
- Non-tangential approach region: a cone-shaped way of approaching a boundary point, not skimming along the boundary.
- Tangent cone and sector angle: geometric measures of how sharply the boundary bends at a point.
- Little-o and big-O notation: ways of saying one quantity is much smaller than, or bounded by a constant times, another as points approach a limit.
summary.one_liner: The paper proves boundary rigidity theorems for holomorphic self-maps of bounded convex domains in C^n, showing that a self-map which agrees with the identity to high order at a boundary point must be the identity, and it proves a conjecture of Zimmer in the non-smooth case.
summary.plain: The paper studies maps that send a region of complex space back into itself in a smooth, complex-differentiable way. It asks: if such a map barely moves points near one point on the region's edge, is it forced to be the do-nothing map everywhere? The authors show that, under the stated conditions, the answer is yes.
summary.why: This is a sharpened version of a classical rigidity result (the Burns-Krantz theorem), and the non-smooth-boundary result is said in the text to prove a conjecture of Zimmer. The text does not say what wider applications it has, so its broader importance is unclear from this text alone.

papers.abstract: We prove two boundary rigidity theorems for holomorphic self-maps of bounded convex domains. Let $Ω\subset\C^n$, $n\geq1$, and suppose that $\partialΩ$ is $C^{1,α}$ near $p\in\partialΩ$ for some $0<α\leq1$. If a holomorphic self-map $f$ satisfies $f(z)=z+o(|z-p|^3)$ as $z\to p$ in one fixed non-tangential approach region at $p$, then $f=\id_Ω$. We also prove a rigidity theorem for bounded convex domains $Ω$ without assuming boundary smoothness. If a holomorphic self-map $f$ of $Ω$ satisfies $f(z)-z=O(|z-p|^m)$ as $z\to p\in\partialΩ$ for some $m>1+2π/θ_p$, where $θ_p$ is the supremum of sector angles in the open tangent cone at $p$, taken over complex lines through its vertex, then $f=\id_Ω$, which proves a conjecture of Zimmer.

papers.title: Singular sets of conformal curves are discrete
papers.label: arXiv:2611.21505v1

summary.background:
- Conformal map: a map that preserves angles locally (here, in the sense defined in the source paper, between Euclidean spaces).
- Differential / full rank: the best linear approximation of the map at a point; full rank means it does not collapse any direction.
- Singular set: the points where the differential fails to have full rank.
- Discrete set: a set whose points are isolated from one another, with no clustering.
- Real-analytic: locally expressible by convergent power series; very smooth.
- Fibers: the sets of inputs that map to the same output.
- Associative, coassociative and Special Lagrangian: special classes of submanifolds from geometric analysis, which the examples concern.
summary.one_liner: The paper shows that the differential of a non-constant conformal curve between Euclidean spaces has full rank outside a discrete set, with consequences for real-analyticity, fibers, and examples of associative, coassociative and Special Lagrangian conformal curves.
summary.plain: The paper studies "conformal curves," maps between spaces of any dimension that preserve angles in a particular sense. It asks where such a map stops being well behaved (where it squashes space down instead of locally stretching it without collapse). The authors find that these bad points are isolated, forming a discrete set, rather than spread over large regions.
summary.why: Knowing that the troublesome points are isolated tells us conformal curves are, outside those points, as smooth and regular as the analysis allows. The text does not say how far the results reach beyond the examples it lists, so broader significance is uncertain.

papers.abstract: We prove that the differential of a non-constant conformal curve between Euclidean spaces has full rank outside a discrete set. In particular, conformal curves are real-analytic outside a discrete set. We provide examples of entire associative and coassociative conformal curves with a non-empty singular set. We show that every non-constant Special Lagrangian conformal curve is a real-analytic conformal immersion. We also prove that a non-constant conformal curve has discrete fibers.

papers.title: Multidimensional mixed Bohr radii for Banach space valued holomorphic functions
papers.label: arXiv:2611.19268v1

summary.background:
- Holomorphic function: a complex-differentiable function, which can be written as a power series.
- Bohr radius: the largest radius r such that a bounded holomorphic function's power series, evaluated inside that radius, stays bounded by the same bound; the classical result is about one-variable functions on the unit disc.
- Banach space: a complete normed vector space; functions here take values in such spaces, not just in numbers.
- Unit ball and Minkowski sequence space: the set of points of size at most one in a finite-dimensional space with a specified norm; the sequence space is the setting for the multidimensional version.
- Bounded linear operator and norm: a structure-preserving map between spaces and a measure of its maximum stretching.
- Cotype: a geometric measure of how "spread out" a Banach space is; finite cotype is a restriction on the space's geometry.
- Banach lattice, concave Banach lattice, summing operator: ordered Banach spaces and a class of operators with good summation properties, used to state the lower bounds.
- Asymptotic behavior: how a quantity behaves as the dimension grows large.
summary.one_liner: The paper defines multidimensional mixed Bohr radii for holomorphic functions on the unit ball of a finite-dimensional Minkowski sequence space with Banach-space values, and studies their positivity, asymptotics under cotype assumptions, and lower bounds for concave Banach lattices and summing operators.
summary.plain: The paper studies a generalized version of the Bohr radius, a classical quantity that measures how far a complex-valued function's power series can be bounded in size while its coefficients stay controlled. Here the functions take values in more general spaces of vectors or operators, and the domain is a higher-dimensional ball. The text reports results on when this radius is positive, how it behaves for large dimensions in spaces of finite cotype (a geometric property of the space), and some lower bounds for concave Banach lattices and summing operators.
summary.why: Bohr radii link complex analysis to coefficient estimates and to the geometry of the underlying space, so the paper's results on how the radius depends on dimension and space geometry may be of interest to specialists in the area. The abstract says the results are consistent with the classical Bohr radius and with sharp Defant–Frerick asymptotics, but I have not checked how these compare with other work in the field.

papers.abstract: In this paper, we introduce and study a generalized notion of multidimensional mixed Bohr radii for holomorphic functions defined on the unit ball of the finite-dimensional Minkowski sequence space with values in complex Banach spaces. We first prove that the multidimensional mixed Bohr radius is positive for every non-null bounded linear operator whose norm is sufficiently small relative to the scaling parameter. We then determine the exact asymptotic behavior of the multidimensional mixed Bohr radius for infinite-dimensional Banach spaces of finite cotype and we obtain analogous bounds for spaces without finite cotype. Finally, for concave Banach lattices and summing operators, we prove lower bounds that involve a logarithmic factor. These results connect classical scalar Bohr phenomena with operator-valued and Banach space valued settings, and highlight how the geometry of the spaces and the mapping properties of the operator influence coefficient estimates and their dependence on dimension. Several examples illustrate the consistency of our results with the classical Bohr radius and the sharp Defant--Frerick asymptotics.
